rv.q: Ms. Nottage, a two-time Pulitzer Prize-winner for drama, and her director, Jo Bonney, have shaped this story with such theatrical inventiveness and discipline that it never feels sensational, on the one hand, or pious, on the other.
The world Nottage has brought to the stage is rich with detail, its characters complex and engaging.

While it's not a revelatory theatrical experience, the show is tightly crafted and engagingly performed, and there's something strangely refreshing about an issue play that's not pretending to be something else.
For Mlima's Tale, the new play by Lynn Nottage at the Public Theater, is monumental.
Eighty straight minutes of searing brilliance...
Nottage is a master at her craft, and so with the estimable contributions of Ngaujah and Bonney, she meets this challenge with great success.
But it is Ngaujah's presence—both tragic and damning—as Mlima himself that is the most commanding on stage.

Bonney’s production enhances the stark and quiet ironies of Nottage’s script with an effective soundscape (by the ever-reliable Darron L. West) that blends with live music (performed onstage by Justin Hicks).
A timely, sorrowful story told very well indeed, Mlima's Tale demonstrates the remarkable versatility of Nottage as a playwright.
Mlima's Tale is a harrowing trip, but well worth taking.
Nottage and director Jo Bonney manage to turn Mlima's Tale into a forceful morality tale without beating the audience over the head.
Sahr Ngaujah gives a captivating performance, poetic in both movement and emotion.
What stays engaging is the beautiful stagecraft – Ngaujah's haunting presence; the nods to African storytelling... the lush lighting... the African-inflected percussive-focused music...
What propels the story forward is Ngaujah's presence.
Mlima's Tale is a play not to be missed.
The glory of Mlima's story is how Nottage and her gifted director, Jo Bonney, tell it in theatrical terms.
Sahr Ngaujah's performance as Mlima and Mlima's Tusks is spellbinding, spiritualistic, and primordially otherworldly.
I do not think I will ever be able to look at a piece of ivory without feeling the horror that accompanies the beauty.

"A highly artistic exposé of a scandalous wildlife dilemma…that fills its…80 minutes with fascinating information contained in dramatically compelling scenes…Ngaujah, gifted with physical and vocal beauty, makes the pachyderm a hauntingly tragic presence; he need merely stand there…for you to feel how deeply he's invested.
